vignette:
Frank is a 69-year-old retired plumber, a slight man with calloused hands and a quiet, watchful way about him. He has been married to his wife, Linh, for forty-seven years. He comes to therapy at her gentle insistence, because for the last three months, he has been unable to enter their basement.

The story begins in April of 1975, in Saigon. Frank was a young man of twenty-two, a newlywed, and a mechanic for the South Vietnamese army. When the city fell, he did not flee. He stayed to try and find his wife’s family. He was captured by the new regime and sent to a re-education camp. That is the clinical term. For Frank, it was a prison. He was held for six years.

He does not speak of the torture. He speaks of the small things. The constant, gnawing hunger. The way the rice was measured out, grain by grain. The smell of the latrine pit, which he can still summon at will. He speaks of the boredom, the terrible, crushing boredom that was its own form of pain. He learned to count the seconds in his head, to pass the time. He can still do it. He will be sitting in the waiting room, and his lips will move silently, counting.

When he was released, he and Linh came to the United States. He became a plumber. He was good at it. He liked the work. It was practical. You saw a leak, you fixed it. A problem had a solution. He worked for forty years, never taking a vacation. He would not fly. He would not go anywhere he could not drive home from in a few hours. He never told his customers about his past. He was just Frank, the plumber who showed up on time and did the job right.

Now he is retired. The retirement was meant to be a reward, a rest. Instead, it has become a trap. Three months ago, his wife asked him to go into the basement to fix a leak in the hot water heater. He walked down the wooden steps. The air was cool and damp. The single bare bulb cast a weak, yellow light. He stood at the bottom, looking at the concrete walls, the low ceiling, the single small window high up, covered in cobwebs. He felt a familiar tightness in his chest. He started to count. One, two, three… He could smell the latrine pit. He could hear the guards shouting in a language he has tried to forget. His hands began to shake. He turned and walked back up the stairs.

He told Linh he was feeling dizzy. The next day, he tried again. The same thing happened. Now, he cannot go down the basement steps at all. He cannot even look at the basement door. He has started checking the locks on the front and back doors three times before he can go to sleep. He has a small, precise ritual: front door, back door, kitchen window. Front door, back door, kitchen window. If he is interrupted, he must start over. He has begun to hoard canned food in the pantry, stacking it in neat, silent rows. He does not know why.

He also has a new, sharp irritability. Last week, a neighbor’s dog barked too long, and Frank found himself standing on his porch, shouting into the dark, his heart hammering, his fists clenched. He was ashamed afterwards. He apologized to the neighbor, but the shame has not faded.

He sits in the therapy office, his hands folded in his lap. He does not make eye contact. He speaks in a low, even voice, as if he is describing a problem with a pipe. He says he does not understand why this is happening now. He survived the camp. He built a life. He fixed a thousand leaks. Why now? He looks at the therapist, and for a moment, his eyes are the eyes of the twenty-two-year-old who was taken. He is a man who has spent a lifetime successfully avoiding the basement of his own mind, and now the door has opened, and he cannot close it.
